body.text: She is already still above him. Her knees are on Sol’s moving blanket on either side of his hips and her fist is shut around the St. Michael where it lies on his chest, and his *wait* arrives late, under her, into a room where she has already stopped. She breathes hard through her nose, in and out, her hair hanging down around both their faces with the red coming through it in strands, and she doesn’t move, and the breath goes on shaking in and out of her as if she’d run here.

She comes up over him, a knee on each side of his hips on Sol’s moving blanket, and reaches down and takes him in her hand. She brings him to her and holds him there, against her, slick and hot at the very edge, and does not come down — the closest the two of them have ever been, and nothing keeping it there but her hand and whatever she does next. His hips come up off the blanket on their own, after her, and she puts her free palm low on his stomach and presses him back down without looking away from his face. Then she goes still. Her breath stops, and starts again, shorter. Her eyes are on his chest: on the bare place on his breastbone, pale in the red, where the medal has hung since his confirmation. She lets go of him. She climbs off the daybed and crosses the little room to the dry counter by the enlarger, naked in the safelight, and lifts the St. Michael off the Formica by its chain, and comes back and drops it over his head herself. It catches on his ear, the way it did coming off. She frees it, and sets it back where it lives with one knuckle, and kneels over him with her hand on it.

She comes up over him, a knee on each side of his hips on Sol’s moving blanket, and reaches down and takes him in her hand. She brings him to her and holds him there, against her, slick and hot at the very edge, and does not come down — the closest the two of them have ever been, and nothing keeping it there but her hand and whatever she does next. His hips come up off the blanket on their own, after her, and she puts her free palm low on his stomach and presses him back down without looking away from his face. Then she goes still. Her breath stops, and starts again, shorter. Her eyes are on his chest, on the St. Michael on its chain on his breastbone, red in the safelight like everything else in here. She lets go of him. Her hand comes up and closes over the medal.
“Not him,” she says, her fist around the medal. “I was never going to take him off you.”
“Not him,” she says. “Don’t take him off for me.”
“Not him,” she says, with the medal in her fist. “I’m not taking him off you.”

body: “No,” she says, in her own voice.
She says it close, into his face, with her hair still hanging down around them both, and afterward her mouth stays a little open, as though the word were bigger going out than it looked.

She lifts away and lies down beside him on Sol’s daybed, on her back under the line, her shoulder against his, and she stays. Their clothes are in one heap on the floor of the dry side, red on red, where she dropped them.

Everything stops with it. Her hands, his, the clock that has been running in both of them since he knocked: all of it stops, and nothing starts up again against the edge to keep the heat going. She has come away from the edge and lain down.

The sweat on his chest goes cold first. Then the backs of his legs, where the moving blanket is rough, and the place on his hip where her knee was. He can smell her on his hands and on his mouth, and the vinegar from the wet side under that, and the hot dust of the safelight. Above them the prints of him hang in a row on their clothespins, the back of him on the Point three times over, getting smaller, and him asleep, and they drip.

His body hasn’t heard. He lies there with his heart going hard enough to shake the iron frame and his hands open on the blanket, and the first thing he knows clearly, before anything else can arrive, is that he would have. The second thing is his breath, coming back into him slower than his heart, from somewhere outside the room, like it’s being returned.

When he can, he turns on his side toward her. She lets him get his arm under her neck. She reaches down for the free half of Sol’s moving blanket and hauls it up over the two of them to the chin, brisk as a nurse, and tucks it in along his back with the side of her hand, and then she lies still under it with her shoulder in his armpit and her eyes open.

On the wet side the timer goes off. It has ticked under everything since he came through the door, and now it rings — a flat tin ring that doesn’t let up — for some print she left in the fixer an hour ago and forgot. They let it ring. It rings until it runs down, and after it the room is quieter than it was before anything started: the needle hissing around the last groove of Sol’s record, and a drop falling from the line over them and landing, small and cold, on the blanket by his hip.
Skye lies looking up at the pictures of him.
“Well,” she says. “That’s never happened to me.”

He turns his head on the blanket. Her profile in the red: the slope of her nose, her mouth still open from breathing, a strand of hair stuck to her temple with sweat, and her eyes wide open on the line.
“You okay?”
“Ask me why,” she says.

So he asks her why. She finds his hand on the blanket and brings it over and puts it on her stomach under her own, where he can feel her breathing go up and down, slower now, and slower, and she takes her time.

s09b.slug: FRIDAY · 12:20 AM · THE DARKROOM — MARY KATE
body: The red can’t change; it’s a bulb on a cord. Over the daybed the prints have slowed to a drop every few minutes, and Sol’s moving blanket is over both of them now, quilted, smelling of a storage unit and faintly of the vinegar from the wet side. Skye lies along him with her head on his shoulder and one foot hooked over his ankle, and she is watching the line.

body.text: Through the propped door the hall runs off dark toward the kitchen, where the stove light is still on over the burners: a little yellow at the far end of the house, the only thing in sight that isn’t red.
body.else: The door is shut where he shut it, the jug of fixer against the wall where his foot put it, and the seam around the door is as red as the rest of the room.

body: “That print in the fixer,” he says. “The one the timer was for.”
“Ruined. Probably. Sol would know.” She doesn’t sound sorry. “It was you again. I’ve got plenty of you.”

“You have somewhere to be in the morning,” she says. “So do I. I said nowhere to be.” Her finger is drawing on his chest under the blanket, slowly, something with corners. “I said it in your room and I meant it, and tonight I changed it because I wanted to. I don’t do that. I don’t say a thing and then not.”
The finger stops.
“And then you said yes.”
He waits for her. The safelight hums on its cord, the only sound in the room.
“I wanted the yes,” she says. “I didn’t know till I had it that it was the part I wanted.”
“The yes,” he says.

“Since November. Since the window seat. I’ve been asking you for it in every room in Santa Barbara County.” Her finger starts again, the corners. “And you gave it to me on a daybed in a closet with your pictures dripping on us. And I had it. And it was —” The finger stops at the end of a corner. “I didn’t need anything after it. I didn’t know that about myself.”

He turns it over and can’t find the bottom of it. Overhead the print of him asleep lets go of a drop, and it lands in her hair. She tips her head back to look up at it — him on her mattress at first light with his ribs bare, upside down from here — and tells it, “You’ve been watching this whole time. Creep.”

To the real one she says, “Look where we are.” Her hand comes out from under the blanket and takes in the room: the bulb, the black cloth tacked over the plywood, the trays, the line of him. “A room built so nobody can see anything in it. Lights off. I said I wanted to be the good thing with the lights off.” The hand goes back under. “I’d still be the thing you tell him about through a screen.”
He starts to say she isn’t, and she puts her fingertips on his mouth.
“Don’t make it nice. You were going to make it nice.”
He was. He lies there with it shut.
“Why the morning?” he says, when she takes the fingers away. “You keep coming back to the morning.”
She’s quiet long enough for two drops to come down off the line. He hears one hit the blanket. The other one he doesn’t hear land.

“He called me Mary Kate,” she says. “My father. Before the Olsens ruined it.” Her cheek moves on his chest; it might be a smile. “Pat Doyle was a juicer. Lights, not oranges — everybody asks. When they shot on location they wanted him there at five, so he left in the dark. That’s most of what I have of him. The dark, and the door, and the truck starting out in the street.” Her hand has gone still on his ribs. “One morning he came in and kissed me in my bed and said go back to sleep, Mary Kate. So I went back to sleep. I was four.”
Somewhere at the front of the house the refrigerator kicks on and hums.

“He didn’t come back,” she says. “Debbie says I made up the kiss. I was four, I don’t remember anything, how would I remember a kiss.” Her thumb moves on his ribs. “I didn’t make it up. He smelled like coffee and the cold.”
“Did you wait up?”
“For a while.” She thinks about it. “Then I got a call time of my own.”
She lifts her head off his chest and looks at him, close, the red on half her face and the other half dark.
“Everybody I’ve ever loved had a call time.”
He gets his hand into her hair and holds the back of her head, the hair still stiff at the roots from the Point.
“Tonight we both have call times, Jack,” she says. “You at five. Me at six-forty.” And she puts her head back down where it was.

So he tells her about the turnout on Highway 1 in August, the first day: his father swinging the Silverado into the gravel without a signal, leaving the engine running and the door open and the dinger going, and walking to the guardrail in his union windbreaker with his hands in his pockets, and standing there looking at the Pacific for the first time in fifty-one years. Not one word. Not then, not in the truck after, not on the phone since. “That’s how you know with him,” Jack says. “When he doesn’t say anything. That’s the most he’s got.”
Skye lies with her ear on his chest and listens to it come up through him.

“And I’ve never had nowhere to be in the morning either,” he says. “Not one I can remember. There’s a shift on Glenwood Avenue, or a Mass, or a bus. My dad’s alarm went off at a quarter to five for twenty-six years.” He hears himself and keeps going. “In June it stopped. He still gets up at a quarter to five. He sits in the garage with the radio.”
“So nobody has to watch him not leave,” she says. And then: “Does he know? That you love him?”
“We don’t say it.” He looks up at the line. “He drove me across the country instead. Two plane tickets cost more than the truck’s worth. Then he drove it home alone.”
“That’s saying it,” Skye says. “That’s saying it with a truck.”
He has one more, and it’s the one he has been holding since the timer rang.
“What would you have done,” he says, “if I’d said no?”

“Asked again.” No hesitation in it at all. “Next week. On the phone from Burnaby, from a trailer. The night you got back. I’d always ask again, Jack. That’s the problem.” Her hand closes in the hair on his chest. “I’d never have stopped. So I did.”
He lies there with that a while. Then he gives her the only thing he has that’s as true as it.
“I’d have let you,” he says. “Tonight. I want you to know it was you. It wasn’t me holding anything.”
“I know.” She doesn’t lift her head. “I was there, Jack. I was the one holding it.”
She lays her cheek on him again, under the line of prints, and talks to his chest.

“When you come back,” she says. “Whatever you’ve got. Whatever happens down there — the Saints, Mardi Gras, a float falls on you. You tell me. To my face.” Her fingers move on his chest. “Not in a text from Texas. You don’t lie. It’s the only reason I can do any of this.”

choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You promised.
response: “Okay,” she says into his chest, and her arm comes across him under Sol’s blanket and settles there. Over them a drop comes off the line and lands on his wrist, and runs off it into the blanket.

choices.text: “I’ll tell you the truth. I always have.”
choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You told her you always have.
response: “I’ll tell you the truth,” he says. “I always have.”

She comes up on an elbow and looks at him in the red. Then she touches the scar through his eyebrow with one fingertip, and goes no further into it than that. Past her shoulder the line runs from the enlarger to the door, and halfway along it, where the swing hung, there’s a clothespin holding nothing.

choices.text: *Take her face in your hands and say yes.*
choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You took her face in your hands and said yes.
response: He takes her face in his hands, both of them, the red on it and the damp hair at her temples under his thumbs, and says yes.

She holds still for it with her eyes open. When he lets go she puts her head back down on his chest, and he lies looking up past her at the timer on the wet-side shelf, its hand stopped where it rang.

choices.text: “The truth is I’m going to be terrible at Mardi Gras.”
choices.key: Skye asked for the truth, to her face, when you come back. You told her you’ll be terrible at Mardi Gras — then, when she waited, you promised.
response: “The truth is,” he says, “I’m going to be terrible at Mardi Gras.”
She lifts her head and looks at him until he says the rest. “I promise.”

“You’re going to be magnificent at Mardi Gras,” Skye says. “That’s what I’m afraid of.” And she laughs at herself, into his collarbone, hard enough that the iron frame creaks and the line of prints shivers over them on its clothespins.

s09c.slug: FRIDAY · 2:25 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — CALL TIMES
body: After the red, her overhead light is an assault: the white ceiling, the blue duvet, his own hands gone pink again. The three suitcases stand zipped by the door, biggest to smallest, a family waiting on a cab. The Saab’s keys sit on top of the jar of beach glass, and her white phone on the dresser says 2:25.

Skye is on the end of the bed in a gray hoodie and bare legs, pulling on socks and reading it off to him like a call sheet. “Santa Barbara at six-forty. San Francisco. Vancouver by lunch. A man at the bottom of the escalator holding a sign with somebody else’s name on it.”
“Passport,” she says, and slaps the front pocket of the hoodie, and it’s there. She’s done that twice since they came up the stairs.

Over her head on the shelf the O’Connor is back in its place, the spine broken white, the one with CON crossed out inside it. The room has been stripped down to what stays: the jar, the books, the bare end of the clothes rack, the window over the bed showing nothing but the room back.

Jack is on the floor with his back against the dresser, lacing his boots. Hale’s *Moviegoer* is in his back pocket with the print inside it. He told her in the hall where he’s going: Osei says whenever you knock; he was a doctor; he’s used to being woken.
“Tell him I said hi,” she says. “Your priest.” She hears it before he’s finished the first boot. “Don’t tell him I said hi. It’ll look like lobbying.”
“He’d take it as lobbying.”
“He’d bless it. He blesses everything. He blessed my candle and I didn’t even ask.” She gets the second sock on and sits with both hands around her ankle, watching him double-knot.
“You’re going to go tell him anyway.”
“I said yes.”
“So the yes counts,” she says. “I read that one. The heart one.”
“The yes is most of it.”
She thinks about that with her chin on her knee. Down the hall Tomás’s door is shut, and two streets over the party has finally given up.
“Then what did I stop?”
He finishes the knot before he answers. “Sunday,” he says. “Me on Sunday, in some church in New Orleans, getting to go up. And the part I’d have had to carry to Louisiana.”
She nods, slowly.
“Okay.”
She stands, crosses the room in her socks, and takes the keys off the jar. The glass in it shifts and settles. She holds the keys in her fist with the fob hanging out, and looks at him on her floor.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked, and I said yes, and she was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised.

choices.text: *Let her drive you up the hill.*

s09h.slug: FRIDAY · 2:45 AM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE LOT UNDER THE BELL TOWER
body: She drove up Ocean Road with the top up and both hands on the wheel and no radio, past the Grove and the dark faculty houses and the turn for the harbor, and said nothing on the way up but “Seat belt,” at the bottom of the hill, the way his mother says it.

The lot under the bell tower holds Osei’s small car by the hall door and, now, the Saab, nosed in beside it with the engine running for the heat. Three suitcases ride in the back seat, belted in. She belted them. The big one has its handle up against the roof like a hand raised in class.
Behind the blue glass of the church a light is on low, over toward the side aisle: small, yellow, steady. Everything else in the building is dark except the red point by the tabernacle.
Skye has her wrists crossed on top of the wheel and her chin on her wrists, and she looks at the light with him. The heater blows on their shins.

He said yes, in a red room, a little over three hours ago. He is about to walk across a parking lot and say so, and she drove him to the door. He looks at her hands on the wheel, the rings, the knuckles, and can’t think of a thing to say about that which wouldn’t be a joke.
“I’ll be here,” she says. “I’m good at waiting in cars. It’s most of my job.” She tips her head at the back seat without lifting her chin. “And I brought company.”
“You could sleep.”
“I could. I won’t.” She turns her face on her wrists to look at him. “Go on. He’s up. Look at him, up.”
He leans across the gearshift to kiss her, and she stops him with one hand on his chest, on the St. Michael through his shirt, not pushing, just there.
“Kiss me coming out.”
He looks at her for that, and she looks back, in the green of the dash lights, with her hand where it is, until he nods. She takes the hand back and folds it on the wheel with the other one.

He gets out. The door shuts on the heater, and the cold coming down off the hill gets into his collar on the first step, and across the lot the light behind the blue glass is still on, waiting for whoever knocks.

s09w.slug: FRIDAY · 2:40 AM · OCEAN ROAD, ON FOOT
body: At the front door she stands on the sill in her socks with the hall light behind her, the porch dark and Sol’s swing hanging still at the end of it. She has his collar in one fist.
“I’ll see you at five,” she says. “I’ll be the one with three suitcases.”
She kisses him there, quick, up on her toes on the sill, and lets go of the collar with a little shove that starts him down the steps.

Del Playa this late is wrecked and quiet: red cups in the ice plant, a couch on a garage roof with a sleeping bag on it, somebody’s bike lying in the street with its front wheel still turning in the wind off the water. Under the bluff the surf breaks and drags its stones back. He goes up through Las Olas past the jasmine on the chain-link, and then the houses stop and the Grove starts, and the eucalyptus is giving its smell up into the cold — menthol, and the other thing, and the rain they haven’t had.

Ocean Road has no shoulder worth the name. He walks the white line. Hale’s *Moviegoer* rides in his back pocket with the print inside it, and every step he can feel the corner of it through the book and the denim, a stiff little edge against his hip.

He said yes. He doesn’t try to make it smaller on the way up. In twenty minutes he’ll have to say it to a man behind a screen, and there’s no other word for what he said than the word he said, so he carries that one up the hill. He starts a Hail Mary under the eucalyptus and loses it at *the fruit of thy womb*, and stands in the road a moment, and starts it over from the top, and gets through.

One car comes up behind him: a pizza Civic with its sign still lit on the roof at this hour, the driver hunched over the wheel like he’s reading it. Its lights throw Jack’s shadow a hundred feet up the road ahead of him and then take it back, and its taillights go around the curve and leave him the dark.

The road climbs. At the top of the hill St. Brendan’s is a black shape against a sky only a little less black, the bell tower going up out of it, and before he has reached the courtyard gate he can see it: one light on behind the blue glass, low, over toward the side aisle, small and yellow, the only lit window on the hill.
